LEARNING PATH LESSON · GARDEN THINGS · AGES 2 YEARS

Rake — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson gathers: your toddler rakes the air like the real thing, drags leaves into piles with their own arms, and earns the grand prize of autumn — the jump-in, supervised and magnificent.

What is this?

A rake is a long-handled tool with a row of teeth at the end, made for pulling leaves into piles. You drag it towards you and the teeth gather everything in their way.

What does it mean?

The rake teaches gathering — a movement toddlers can rehearse with nothing but an arm. It also sets up the season’s great collaboration: the grown-up rakes, the toddler quality-checks, everybody jumps.

What does the child need to know?

A rake’s spiky row of teeth sweeps leaves up into heaps, and it is another grown-up tool — the metal ones stay in the shed. The arm version works anywhere, and the leaf pile’s true purpose is jumping, with a grown-up watching.

Why this matters

Raking the air is whole-arm coordination dressed as play, and the pile is the payoff that makes gathering feel worthwhile. The tool rule repeats what the shovel taught: big tools, grown-up hands.

What it teaches

Dragging and gathering arm movements, autumn awareness (leaves fall, then piles happen), jump-and-land control, tool-versus-arm sorting, and the deep joy of a job with a jump at the end.

Words to learn

rakeleavesteethpilegatherjump

Say this to your child

“"A rake! Scratch, scratch — its long teeth pull all the leaves into a big pile. Can you rake the air with me? Drag, drag, gather... The real rake is a grown-up tool, but your arm is a very good rake too. And when the pile is ready — you know what comes next. Jump!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card, say rake, and drag your arm along the floor — scratch, scratch — pulling an invisible pile towards you.
  2. Rake the air together, gathering make-believe leaves — then gather some real ones off the floor into one big heap.
  3. Point out the teeth on the card: a row of them, all working at once — that is how the rake gathers so much in one drag.
  4. Say the tool rule: the real rake belongs to grown-ups, the same as the shovel — your rake is your arm, and it works brilliantly.
  5. Promise the finale: when the grown-up rake makes a real pile in autumn, jumping in it is the toddler’s official job — one jump, two jumps!

Look closer at the picture

Drag one arm slowly across the rug and say rake. Ask your toddler to find the teeth on the card — the spiky row — then gather cushions into a pile with raking arms, scratch by scratch.

Ask your child

"What does the rake gather?" "How many teeth does a rake have — one or lots?" "Who uses the real rake?" "What do we do with the pile when it is ready?" — answered with a drag, "lots!", "grown-ups!" and a two-footed answer to the last one.

What your child can say or do

"Scratch scratch!" Expect air-raking in queues and kitchens, leaves herded into piles on every autumn walk, and jump-in requests at every pile seen. The arm-rake may be deployed to gather toys — accept gratefully.

Out in the real world

Rakes work lawns, parks and gutters all autumn, and leaf piles appear wherever trees do. Each pile is a rerun — rake arms, gather, admire — and the big jumps stay strictly in the grown-up-made piles.

Try it together

Leaf pile at home: scatter paper or fabric leaves, rake them together with arms into one heap, count the jumps over it, then rake again. Repeat until the pile or the toddler is fully autumn.

Understanding check

At the next leaf-fall, watch the arms: gathering motions aimed at a pile mean the rake has moved in. The tool rule said back unprompted — "grown-up rake!" — finishes the lesson.

Parent tips

Rake a jumping pile yourself this autumn and stand back — the delight is the lesson’s certificate. Keep the air-rake gentle around lamps and siblings; teeth are pretend but enthusiasm is real.

Staying safe

Real rakes have hard teeth and long handles that swing — grown-up custody, same as the shovel, and nobody walks behind a working rake. Jump-in piles get one pre-jump check from you: sticks, holes and hidden garden forks removed first.

This lesson pairs with the Rake flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Things (School Garden).
